record.title: Single customer account + single IP can saturate all gunicorn gthreads via replayable SSE tickets (full-API DoS)
record.description: GET /api/customer/notifications/stream/ is AllowAny and authenticated solely by a replayable signed ticket, throttled only by CustomerPublicReadThrottle (scope 'public_read' = 1000/hour per IP). Each SSE connection consumes exactly one throttle token at check_throttles time and then occupies one gunicorn gthread for up to STREAM_MAX_SECONDS=50s (bounded below only by client disconnect, detected on the next ≤15s ping write). The whole API shares workers=3 × threads=4 = 12 concurrent request handlers (docker/api/gunicorn.conf.py:14-16; compose/.env.example 3×4, Render blueprint 2×4=8 — even easier). Sustained saturation needs ~N×3600/50 connection-opens/hour (864 for 12 threads, 576 for 8) — inside the 1000/hour per-IP budget with ~14-42% headroom, and a fresh burst of up to 1000 requests is allowed instantly by the sliding-window throttle. Because tickets carry no jti (customers-sse:ticket-replay-no-epoch), ONE ticket authorizes unlimited concurrent streams during its 120s TTL; ~720 ticket-mints/day per account covers continuous operation, under the 'user'=1000/day stream-ticket budget — so a single self-registered customer account (registration issues a working JWT immediately, email_verified not required) plus one source IP suffices for indefinite full-API denial of service for every tenant, storefront, auth endpoint and admin path.
record.root_cause: The SSE endpoint was given the generic public-read throttle (1000/hour/IP, sized for cheap request/response reads) instead of a bound proportional to connection-hold cost: a stream request is not a read, it is a 50-second worker-thread lease. No per-customer/per-IP concurrent-stream counter exists, and the ticket's replayability within its 120s TTL makes per-connection credential cost ~zero.
record.intended_behavior: A long-lived connection endpoint must bound concurrent holds, not just request rate: a dedicated throttle scope sized for the feature plus a cache-backed in-flight counter (e.g. max 2-4 open streams per customer+IP), single-use or near-single-use tickets, and/or an nginx limit_conn on the stream route.

conditions.description: Attacker needs one customer account: POST /api/customer-auth/register/ is AllowAny self-service issuing an immediate JWT ('register' throttle 10/hour/IP is irrelevant — one account suffices). No platform (auth.User) account or email verification needed.

Deployed concurrency = GUNICORN_WORKERS×GUNICORN_THREADS. Both documented configs fall below the single-IP saturation threshold (3×4=12 needs ~864 conn/hour; 2×4=8 needs ~576 — both < 1000/hour). A larger env override would raise the bar but the endpoint still lacks any dedicated concurrency bound.
All traffic from a single IP — the throttle ident pins REMOTE_ADDR|last-XFF so header spoofing cannot rotate the bucket; no per-IP connection cap exists at nginx or Caddy.

Sustained scripted hold: open N≥thread-count concurrent streams, re-GET before each ~50s server close while the ticket is <120s old, mint a fresh ticket ~every 120s (~720/day < 1000/day 'user' budget).

execution.attacker_perspective: Unauthenticated internet user who self-registers one buyer account and runs a small script holding SSE sockets.
payloads: GET /api/customer/notifications/stream/?ticket=<T>&store=  — repeated ×N concurrent; re-issue every ~45s while ticket age <120s; mint a new ticket via stream-ticket when it expires
instructions: 1. Register one customer account (open endpoint, JWT returned immediately).
2. Mint one stream ticket (replayable for 120s — unlimited concurrent GETs allowed with the same ticket).
3. Open ≥12 (or ≥8 on Render) concurrent GET /api/customer/notifications/stream/?ticket=<T> connections; each holds a gthread ~50s.
4. Cycle: re-open connections before each 'bye'/50s close using the same ticket until it nears 120s, then mint a new ticket (~every 2 minutes → ~720/day, under the 1000/day 'user' throttle).

5. Result: all gunicorn gthreads permanently occupied by streams → every other API request (all storefronts, auth, orders, admin) queues in the gunicorn backlog and times out at nginx (proxy_read_timeout 60s) for the duration of the attack.
execution.observed_result: Source-traced end-to-end: throttle math (1000/hour/IP budget vs ~864-1000 needed holds/hour for 8-12 threads), thread-hold semantics of StreamingHttpResponse under gthread, replayable ticket removing per-connection credential cost, absence of any concurrency cap in view/nginx/Caddy/gunicorn config, and immediate-JWT open registration. No runtime test performed (source-only constraint).

remediation.strategy: Bound concurrent holds, not just request rate: (1) dedicated throttle scope for the stream endpoint (e.g. 'customer_notifications_stream' ~120-240/hour per customer+IP) PLUS a cache-backed in-flight semaphore (max ~3 open streams per customer+IP, acquired on connect / released on generator close); (2) make tickets effectively single-use or few-use by embedding a jti consumed from cache at connect (the frontend already re-mints a ticket per connection, so single-use breaks nothing); (3) bind tickets to the session epoch (tokens_valid_after) and re-check customer.is_active inside _events; (4) optionally add nginx limit_conn on /api/customer/notifications/stream/ as a second layer.

likelihood.reason: Trivially executable by any internet user: open self-registration yields an immediate JWT, one ticket covers unlimited concurrent streams for 120s, and ~720 mints/day sustain the attack under the 1000/day 'user' budget — all from a single IP.

impact.reason: While sustained, all 8-12 gunicorn gthreads are leased by SSE generators, so EVERY API endpoint for ALL tenants (storefronts, catalog, orders, customer and platform auth, admin) stalls behind the gunicorn backlog until nginx/proxy timeouts fire — a full multi-tenant availability kill for the price of one account.

confidence.reason: Every link verified in current source: throttle scope/rate/keying, fail-open mixin, 50s hold, 3×4 and 2×4 worker configs, replayable ticket, immediate-JWT registration, and absence of limit_conn/limit_req on the route. record.title: Stream ticket is a replayable, session-unbound bearer credential transmitted in the URL query (120s window)
record.description: The SSE credential is signing.dumps({'c': customer_pk, 's': slug}, salt='customer-notifications-stream') verified with max_age=TICKET_TTL=120. Verified sub-claims: (1) REPLAYABLE — the payload carries no jti/nonce and nothing is consumed at verify time, so one ticket authorizes unlimited concurrent stream connections for its full 120s TTL (this is also the multiplier that makes customers-sse:worker-exhaustion cheap). (2) NO EPOCH BINDING — the signed material contains only customer pk and slug; the customer session-epoch mechanism that exists for JWTs (customer.tokens_valid_after vs token iat, authentication.py:28-41) is not consulted, so password-reset revocation does not kill outstanding tickets and deactivation is only checked once at connect. (3) is_active NOT RE-CHECKED — Customer.objects.filter(pk, is_active=True) runs once in get() (line 167); the _events loop (lines 187-215) iterates customer_id forever, so a deactivated/deleted customer keeps receiving their own notification stream until the 50s deadline. (4) QUERY-STRING CREDENTIAL — the frontend builds the EventSource URL as ?ticket=<signed>&store=<slug> (customerNotifications.api.js:32-35); the ticket therefore lands in nginx/gunicorn access logs (gunicorn accesslog='-', nginx default combined format) and any proxy/log pipeline. Correction to the hunter's framing: EventSource does not create browser-history entries, so exposure is via server/proxy access logs and any client that records request URLs — still a bearer credential in a URL (CWE-598). Impact is bounded: read-only access to that customer's own notifications for ≤120s per captured ticket, plus a ≤50s post-deactivation tail; the legitimate client already re-mints a ticket per connection (useCustomerNotifications.js:48), so single-use tickets would not break it.
record.root_cause: The stream ticket was designed as a minimal signed tuple {customer, slug}+TTL. It omits a single-use jti, omits binding to the session epoch (tokens_valid_after) used by the JWT path, performs the liveness check only at connect time, and is transported in the URL query string because EventSource cannot set Authorization headers.
record.intended_behavior: A bearer credential for a live-data stream should be single-use (or few-use) within its TTL, bound to the session epoch so logout/password-reset revokes it, re-validate principal liveness periodically inside the stream, and avoid persisting the credential in access logs where practical (e.g. short TTL + jti, or a one-time code exchanged for a cookie-scoped stream).

remediation.strategy: Make the ticket single-use and epoch-bound, and re-validate liveness inside the stream: embed a random jti recorded in cache (cache.add/delete at connect — frontend already re-mints per connection so single-use is free), sign the customer's tokens_valid_after (or a session id) into the payload and compare at connect, re-check customer.is_active inside _events every ~15s alongside the ping, and consider shortening TICKET_TTL to ~30-60s. Optionally move the credential out of the query string (e.g. POST-minted one-time code → short-lived cookie) or ensure access logs for this route redact the query.

record.title: Django 5.2 GZipMiddleware buffers the entire SSE stream — events and heartbeats only reach the client at ~50s stream close
record.description: GZipMiddleware is enabled (DaventProject/settings.py:241) and the pinned runtime is Django==5.2.18 (requirements.txt:17), installed verbatim into both deploy images (docker/api/Dockerfile stages builder/runtime; render.yaml uses the same dockerfilePath). Verified against the Django stable/5.2.x release-branch source (the branch 5.2.18 is tagged from; the per-chunk flush fix, PR #20401 merged 2026-03-09, is absent from stable/5.2.x HEAD and therefore from every 5.2.x release): GZipMiddleware.process_response wraps response.streaming_content in compress_sequence whenever the request's Accept-Encoding contains 'gzip' and no Content-Encoding is set — with no content-type exemption, so text/event-stream is compressed. compress_sequence writes each SSE frame via zfile.write() but never calls zfile.flush(); zlib withholds output until its pending buffer reaches ~16-17KB (documented in the Django commit that removed the flush: 'the buffer is being flushed every 17k or so') or until the GzipFile context closes. The stream's frames are tens-to-hundreds of bytes (': conectado', ': ping' every 15s, small JSON events), so for any realistic notification volume NOTHING is emitted — not even response headers, since WSGI sends headers with the first body bytes — until either ~17KB accumulates or the generator ends at STREAM_MAX_SECONDS=50 and the gzip trailer flushes everything at once. Consequence: browsers (which always send Accept-Encoding: gzip on EventSource) receive the whole 50s of events/heartbeats in a single burst at reconnect time; the 'unread'/'notification' events effectively degrade to ~50s polling granularity and the 15s heartbeat cannot serve its liveness purpose. The view's X-Accel-Buffering:no only affects nginx proxy buffering and does not prevent Django-side gzip; nginx gzip_types excludes text/event-stream so nginx neither re-compresses nor helps; Caddy has no encode directive and passes the upstream Content-Encoding:gzip through.
record.root_cause: django.middleware.gzip.GZipMiddleware unconditionally gzip-compresses sync streaming responses via django.utils.text.compress_sequence, and in Django 5.2.x compress_sequence performs zfile.write() per chunk without zfile.flush(), so zlib buffers the stream until ~17KB pending or close — defeating the real-time delivery contract of text/event-stream.
record.intended_behavior: SSE responses must reach the wire per chunk. Either bypass compression for text/event-stream (skip GZipMiddleware for that content type / set an explicit identity encoding the middleware respects) or run a Django version whose compress_sequence flushes per chunk (fix present on main/6.0 line; verify 5.2.x backport status before upgrading).

trace.description: 'django.middleware.gzip.GZipMiddleware' enabled for all responses including the SSE stream

StreamingHttpResponse(self._events(...), content_type='text/event-stream'); sets Cache-Control:no-cache and X-Accel-Buffering:no (nginx-only hint) but NO Content-Encoding — so GZipMiddleware will compress it for gzip-accepting clients

for response.streaming (sync): response.streaming_content = compress_sequence(response.streaming_content, ...) whenever re_accepts_gzip matches HTTP_ACCEPT_ENCODING and no Content-Encoding header exists — no content-type check exempts text/event-stream

for item in sequence: zfile.write(item); data = buf.read(); yield if data — NO zfile.flush() per chunk; zlib emits only at ~16-17KB pending or at GzipFile.__exit__ (stream close at ~50s) → entire SSE session buffered into one burst

evidence.description: GZipMiddleware present in MIDDLEWARE
Django==5.2.18 — the pinned runtime for both deploy paths
pip install --no-index -r requirements.txt → deployed Django is exactly 5.2.18 (compose api/celery/migrate and Render docker runtime alike)
response['X-Accel-Buffering']='no' — disables nginx proxy buffering only; does not set Content-Encoding, so Django gzip still applies
proxy_read_timeout 60s — upstream silence for ~50s stays under the limit, so the buffered stream still completes (barely)
nginx gzip_types excludes text/event-stream — nginx does not gzip SSE itself, but passes through the upstream Content-Encoding:gzip unchanged

compress_sequence lacks zfile.flush() per chunk — verified on the stable/5.2.x release branch; upstream fix PR django/django#20401 (ticket #36293, 'buffer is being flushed every 17k or so') merged 2026-03-09 is absent from stable/5.2.x HEAD
process_response wraps sync streaming_content in compress_sequence with no content-type exemption; requires only 'gzip' in Accept-Encoding (sent by all browsers for EventSource)

conditions.description: GZipMiddleware enabled (default in this repo) and client sends Accept-Encoding:gzip — true for every browser EventSource; non-gzip clients (e.g. curl without --compressed) bypass compression entirely and see correct streaming.

Typical notification volume keeps each 50s stream well under ~17KB of SSE frames, so nothing flushes before close; a burst >~17KB (e.g. large catch-up payloads) could emit mid-stream but events still arrive late and batched.
Buffered upstream silence lasts until ~50s stream end; nginx proxy_read_timeout is 60s so the response still completes — headroom is only ~10s.

execution.attacker_perspective: Not attacker-driven — a deterministic defect affecting every legitimate SSE client.
payloads: GET /api/customer/notifications/stream/?ticket=<T>&store=<slug> with Accept-Encoding: gzip (default browser EventSource behavior)
instructions: 1. Open the stream as the SPA does (EventSource → ticket → GET stream).

2. Trigger or wait for a customer notification; observe that no 'notification'/'unread' event arrives in real time — all buffered frames plus the final 'bye' are delivered in one burst when the generator closes at ~50s.
3. Confirm response headers (Content-Encoding:gzip) arrive only with that first burst, since WSGI emits headers with the first non-empty body chunk.
execution.observed_result: Source-traced: middleware chain, pinned-version library code on the release branch, and the absence of any Content-Encoding/content-type bypass prove the buffering path; the ~17KB zlib threshold is documented by Django developers in the fix commit. Not observed on a live instance (source-only review; no venv present in the workspace to byte-inspect the installed package — the stable/5.2.x branch source stands in for the 5.2.18 wheel).

remediation.strategy: Exempt text/event-stream from gzip compression: replace 'django.middleware.gzip.GZipMiddleware' with a subclass that returns the response untouched when Content-Type starts with 'text/event-stream' (the Django ticket itself recommends this), or set an explicit no-op Content-Encoding the middleware respects. Alternatively/Additionally upgrade Django once the compress_sequence flush fix is backported to the deployed 5.2.x line (fix is on main; verify release notes). The heartbeat/liveness design then works as intended and events arrive per chunk.

likelihood.reason: Deterministic for every gzip-accepting client — i.e. every real browser running the SPA's EventSource; no attacker action or special config needed.

impact.reason: Customer notifications degrade from push to ~50s batched delivery and heartbeats cannot serve liveness; a security-adjacent timeliness defect, not a trust-boundary crossing — data still arrives, just late, and the 50s<60s timeout margins keep streams alive.

confidence.reason: Full code path proven from repo source plus the pinned Django 5.2.x release-branch source of gzip.py/text.py (no local venv exists to byte-inspect the installed wheel, and no live instance was tested per constraints). Residual uncertainty is limited to the exact zlib emission threshold — immaterial, since any threshold ≫ SSE frame size produces the same buffer-until-close outcome — and to whether a future 5.2.x backport changes the picture (irrelevant: the pin is ==5.2.18).
